title: Kay Hagan Tick Reauthorization Act

claims.claim: The 2019 Kay Hagan Tick Act created two federal programs aimed at tick-borne and other vector-borne diseases
claims.sourceSpan: national strategy to address vector-borne diseases, including tick-borne diseases
claims.note: Both programs added Dec. 20, 2019 by Pub. L. 116-94 per ref codification notes.

claims.claim: The two programs are at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
claims.sourceSpan: in coordination with the Director of the Centers for Disease Control
claims.note: Gloss: the national strategy is the Secretary’s (HHS-wide) with CDC coordination/acting-through; not strictly “at the CDC.” Reasonable simplification, low impact.

claims.claim: Program one is a national strategy plus regional centers of excellence (PHS Act §317U)
claims.sourceSpan: regional centers of excellence in vector-borne diseases

claims.claim: Program two is cooperative agreements with state, local, and tribal health departments in high-risk areas (PHS Act §2822)
claims.sourceSpan: may enter into cooperative agreements with health departments of States, political subdivisions of States, and Indian Tribes and Tribal organizations in areas at high risk of vector-borne diseases

claims.claim: Both programs’ authorizations of appropriations ran through fiscal year 2025
claims.sourceSpan: $10,000,000 for each of fiscal years 2021 through 2025

claims.claim: This bill extends both authorizations through fiscal year 2030
claims.sourceSpan: 2026 through 2030

claims.claim: The bill drops the requirement that HHS consult the Tick-Borne Disease Working Group when developing the national strategy
claims.sourceSpan: the Tick-Borne Disease Working Group

claims.claim: The bill changes CDC’s role in the centers-of-excellence program from coordinating with HHS to acting through HHS
claims.sourceSpan: The Secretary, acting through the Director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
claims.note: Inverted actor: the statute makes the Secretary (HHS) act THROUGH the CDC Director (“The Secretary, acting through the Director of the CDC”), i.e. HHS acts through CDC. Summary says CDC “acting through HHS,” flipping who is the operating arm. top_lines[2]/sections item[2] state it correctly.

claims.claim: Extends the two programs through fiscal year 2030
claims.sourceSpan: 2026 through 2030

claims.claim: The two programs are CDC vector-borne disease programs
claims.sourceSpan: The Secretary, acting through the Director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
claims.note: Both programs involve CDC (coordination / acting-through); “CDC programs” is a defensible gloss though the national strategy is the Secretary’s.

claims.claim: The bill trims two consultation and coordination requirements from the underlying statute
claims.sourceSpan: in coordination with
claims.note: Two non-year changes: strike Working Group from consultation (b); change “in coordination with” to “acting through” (c).

claims.claim: 5-year Extension of Two Vector-borne Disease Programs
claims.sourceSpan: 2026 through 2030
claims.note: FY2026–2030 = 5 fiscal years; both programs.

claims.claim: National strategy + centers of excellence: reauthorized fiscal years 2026 through 2030
claims.sourceSpan: 2026 through 2030

claims.claim: State/local health department cooperative agreements: reauthorized fiscal years 2026 through 2030
claims.sourceSpan: 2026 through 2030

claims.claim: Underlying authorized amounts are $10M (§317U) and $20M (§2822) per year respectively, unchanged in this bill
claims.sourceSpan: $10,000,000 for each of fiscal years 2021 through 2025
claims.note: $20M receipt: “$20,000,000 for each of fiscal years 2021 through 2025” in 300hh-32(c). Bill amends only the year range, not amounts.

claims.claim: Tick-Borne Disease Working Group Dropped from Consultation List
claims.sourceSpan: the Tick-Borne Disease Working Group

claims.claim: Statute previously required consulting the Tick-Borne Disease Working Group established under section 2062 of the 21st Century Cures Act
claims.sourceSpan: shall consult with the Tick-Borne Disease Working Group established under section 284s of this title and other individuals, as appropriate
claims.note: Bill quotes the struck text as “section 2062 of the 21st Century Cures Act (42 U.S.C. 284s)”; codified USC renders it “section 284s of this title.” Same provision.

claims.claim: Bill strikes that requirement and inserts “appropriate individuals”
claims.sourceSpan: appropriate individuals

claims.claim: The Working Group’s authorization has otherwise lapsed — 42 U.S.C. §284s(c)(7) sunsets it 6 years after December 13, 2016
claims.sourceSpan: The Working Group under this section shall terminate 6 years after December 13, 2016.
claims.note: “Lapsed” is derivable: 6 years after 2016-12-13 = 2022, now past.

claims.claim: CDC Role Language Change
claims.sourceSpan: in coordination with

claims.claim: Statute directed HHS to award centers-of-excellence grants “in coordination with” the CDC Director
claims.sourceSpan: in coordination with the Director of the Centers for Disease Control

claims.claim: Bill changes it to “acting through” the CDC Director
claims.sourceSpan: acting through

claims.claim: Signals CDC leads the grant program rather than being a coordinating partner
claims.sourceSpan: The Secretary, acting through the Director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
claims.note: Hedged interpretation (“Signals”) of “acting through”; grounded in internal use of the phrase (300hh-32(a)) but the “leads” conclusion is inferential. Note: direction here (CDC more central) is correct — the opposite of the summary’s inversion.

claims.claim: Section 2 — Reauthorization of Programs
claims.sourceSpan: SEC. 2. REAUTHORIZATION OF PROGRAMS.

claims.claim: Reauthorizes PHS Act §317U (42 U.S.C. 247b-23), which underwrites HHS’s national vector-borne disease strategy and regional centers of excellence
claims.sourceSpan: regional centers of excellence in vector-borne diseases

claims.claim: The underlying statute authorizes $10M per year for fiscal years 2021 through 2025 for these activities
claims.sourceSpan: $10,000,000 for each of fiscal years 2021 through 2025

claims.claim: This bill strikes “2021 through 2025” and inserts “2026 through 2030” — a straight 5-year extension without changing the dollar level
claims.sourceSpan: 2021 through 2025
claims.note: No dollar amendment in bill text.

claims.claim: Removes the requirement that HHS consult the Tick-Borne Disease Working Group in developing the national strategy
claims.sourceSpan: the Tick-Borne Disease Working Group
claims.note: Subsection (b) consultation is “in carrying out subsection (a)(1)” = the national strategy.

claims.claim: The statute’s consultation list (subsection (b)) previously started with the Tick-Borne Disease Working Group established under section 2062 of the 21st Century Cures Act and other individuals, as appropriate
claims.sourceSpan: shall consult with the Tick-Borne Disease Working Group established under section 284s of this title and other individuals, as appropriate
claims.note: Quoted phrase matches the bill’s struck text verbatim.

claims.claim: The bill replaces that phrase with “appropriate individuals,” leaving the enumerated categories (epidemiologists, patient advocates, entomologists, clinicians, researchers) intact
claims.sourceSpan: epidemiologists with experience in vector-borne diseases
claims.note: Bill strikes only the matter preceding paragraph (1); enumerated (1)-(5) untouched. Parenthetical list is illustrative (omits HIT experts, cat (3)).

claims.claim: Changes CDC’s role in the centers-of-excellence grant program from “in coordination with” to “acting through”
claims.sourceSpan: acting through

claims.claim: Under the statute, HHS awards regional centers-of-excellence grants “in coordination with” the CDC Director
claims.sourceSpan: in coordination with the Director of the Centers for Disease Control

claims.claim: The bill substitutes “acting through,” a phrase used elsewhere in public health law to indicate CDC is the operating arm executing the Secretary’s authority
claims.sourceSpan: The Secretary, acting through the Director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
claims.note: Mild generalization; internally grounded — 300hh-32(a) uses “acting through the Director of the CDC.”

claims.claim: Reauthorizes PHS Act §2822 (42 U.S.C. 300hh-32), which lets CDC enter cooperative agreements with state, local, and tribal health departments in high-risk areas for vector-borne disease surveillance and response
claims.sourceSpan: may enter into cooperative agreements with health departments of States, political subdivisions of States, and Indian Tribes and Tribal organizations in areas at high risk of vector-borne diseases
claims.note: “Surveillance and response” glosses “identify, report, prevent, and respond.”

claims.claim: The underlying statute authorizes $20M per year for fiscal years 2021 through 2025 for these cooperative agreements
claims.sourceSpan: $20,000,000 for each of fiscal years 2021 through 2025

claims.claim: This bill strikes “2021 through 2025” and inserts “2026 through 2030”
claims.sourceSpan: 2026 through 2030

claims.claim: Introduced by Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME) with 23 cosponsors
claims.sourceSpan: To reauthorize the Kay Hagan Tick Act, and for other purposes.
claims.note: Sponsor/cosponsor counts are cache metadata (structural), not bill-text facts; permitted for likelihoodReason.

claims.claim: This narrow reauthorization keeps two existing CDC vector-borne disease programs running through fiscal year 2030 at their currently authorized levels
claims.sourceSpan: 2026 through 2030
claims.note: Amounts unchanged in bill.

claims.claim: The two programs are the national tick-borne strategy and state health department cooperative agreements
claims.sourceSpan: national strategy to address vector-borne diseases, including tick-borne diseases
claims.note: “National tick-borne strategy” narrows the statutory “vector-borne diseases, including tick-borne” to tick-borne only; minor imprecision.

claims.claim: The bill passed the Senate by voice/unanimous-consent-style engrossment on August 6, 2026 and now awaits House action
claims.sourceSpan: Passed the Senate August 6, 2026.
claims.note: Voice Vote per votes[]; “unanimous-consent-style” is characterization but grounded in voice-vote method.

claims.claim: Its short length, tight scope, and prior-Congress base statute (the 2019 Kay Hagan Tick Act) place it in the category of low-cost public health reauthorizations that typically move without controversy
claims.sourceSpan: To reauthorize the Kay Hagan Tick Act, and for other purposes.
claims.note: Base statute 2019 is sourced; “low-cost… typically move without controversy” is unsourced category framing (soft). Voice-vote passage of THIS bill is consistent, but the generalization is not sourced.

claims.claim: The consultation requirement removed by this bill is HHS’s obligation to consult the Tick-Borne Disease Working Group when developing the national vector-borne disease strategy
claims.sourceSpan: shall consult with the Tick-Borne Disease Working Group established under section 284s of this title and other individuals, as appropriate

claims.claim: The bill’s short title is a straight “reauthorization,” but the amendment detaches the national strategy from the Working Group
claims.sourceSpan: the Tick-Borne Disease Working Group

claims.claim: The Tick-Borne Disease Working Group is named for Sen. Hagan’s tick-borne disease work
claims.sourceSpan: to be known as the Tick-Borne Disease Working Group
claims.note: The Working Group is the “Tick-Borne Disease Working Group,” established by the 21st Century Cures Act (Pub. L. 114-255, Dec. 13, 2016) — NOT named for Kay Hagan and predating the 2019 Kay Hagan Tick Act. Only the Act bears Hagan’s name; the Working Group does not.

claims.claim: 42 U.S.C. 247b-23(f) authorization of appropriations extended from FY2021–2025 to FY2026–2030
claims.sourceSpan: 2026 through 2030

claims.claim: 42 U.S.C. 247b-23(b) Tick-Borne Disease Working Group consultation requirement replaced with “appropriate individuals”
claims.sourceSpan: appropriate individuals

claims.claim: 42 U.S.C. 247b-23(c) CDC role changed from “in coordination with” to “acting through”
claims.sourceSpan: in coordination with

claims.claim: 42 U.S.C. 300hh-32(c) authorization of appropriations extended from FY2021–2025 to FY2026–2030
claims.sourceSpan: Section 2822(c) of the Public Health Service

claims.claim: The bill extends both authorizations of appropriations but does not itself appropriate any money; funding still depends on the annual Labor-HHS appropriations bill
claims.sourceSpan: $10,000,000 for each of fiscal years 2021 through 2025
claims.note: Authorization vs. appropriation distinction is in source language. “Labor-HHS appropriations bill” is extrinsic civics context (not named in source) — minor.

claims.claim: The bill removes the Working Group from HHS’s consultation requirement but does not repeal, extend, or otherwise address the Working Group established under section 2062 of the 21st Century Cures Act
claims.sourceSpan: to be known as the Tick-Borne Disease Working Group
claims.note: Bill touches only 247b-23(b); §284s (the Working Group) is untouched.

claims.claim: The bill does not update either program’s substantive requirements (eligible entities, reporting, evaluation); changes are limited to authorization years and two consultation/coordination clauses
claims.sourceSpan: SEC. 2. REAUTHORIZATION OF PROGRAMS.
claims.note: Bill amends only 247b-23 (b),(c),(f) and 300hh-32(c); eligibility/reports subsections untouched.

claims.claim: The bill changes CDC’s role from “in coordination with” to “acting through” without addressing whether existing centers-of-excellence grants must be renegotiated
claims.sourceSpan: acting through
claims.note: Bill text is silent on transition of existing grants (absence claim).

notes: Bill is a short engrossed reauthorization (SEC.2 amends 42 U.S.C. 247b-23 (b),(c),(f) and 300hh-32(c)); audited against bill text + 3 registered referencedSources (247b-23, 300hh-32, 284s). No divisions[]. featured_quotes[] (Collins CR floor statement) NOT audited — no Congressional Record source is registered, so it is outside bill-source scope. Two material findings: (1) summary inverts the “acting through” actor (says CDC acts through HHS; statute has the Secretary/HHS acting through CDC); (2) underreported.why_unreported wrongly states the Tick-Borne Disease Working Group is “named for Sen. Hagan” — it is the Tick-Borne Disease Working Group established by the 21st Century Cures Act (2016), not named for Hagan. Coverage/omission: all bill provisions are described; no material omissions.
